# Solving a Two-Bidder Asymmetric First-Price Auction

Yes. There is a general method for solving the first-price sealed-bid auction with exactly two risk-neutral bidders whose independent private values come from different distributions. Under the usual smoothness and monotonicity assumptions, equilibrium is characterized by two coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations for the bidders’ inverse bidding functions. Those equations, together with lower- and upper-endpoint conditions, form a boundary-value problem that can usually be solved numerically. A universal closed-form pair of direct bidding functions does not exist for arbitrary distributions, although important special cases—especially two uniform distributions—can be solved analytically.

The key distinction is therefore between a general equilibrium characterization and a general closed-form formula. The former is available; the latter is not.

## Roadmap

The analysis proceeds in five stages. First, it fixes the exact two-bidder independent-private-values model and states the assumptions under which the standard method applies. Second, it derives the expected-payoff problem, first-order conditions, inverse-bid equations, and boundary conditions. Third, it turns those equations into a practical analytical or numerical recipe and explains how to validate a computed solution. Fourth, it discusses existence, uniqueness, unequal supports, endpoint singularities, and cases in which the standard pure-strategy method needs modification. Finally, it works through asymmetric uniform distributions, compares them with the symmetric benchmark, and places the method in its historical and current scholarly context.

## 1. The exact model and the direct answer

Consider one indivisible object and two bidders, \(i=1,2\). Each simultaneously submits a sealed bid. The highest bid wins and the winner pays her own bid. If bids tie, the winner is selected according to a specified tie-breaking rule, conventionally uniformly at random. Bidder \(i\) observes her own value \(v_i\), but not the other bidder’s value.

The values are independent:

\[
v_1\sim F_1,\qquad v_2\sim F_2,
\]

where \(F_1\neq F_2\) represents ex-ante asymmetry. The difference is known before the auction: bidder identities, the distributions, the supports, the auction rules, and the independence assumption are common knowledge. The realized values remain private information. This is the standard two-bidder asymmetric independent-private-values, or IPV, first-price auction studied in the asymmetric-auction literature ([Maskin and Riley’s model](https://www.isid.ac.in/~dmishra/topicsdoc/maskin_riley.pdf)).

The baseline assumptions are:

| Element | Baseline assumption | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Preferences | Risk-neutral, quasi-linear payoff \(v_i-b_i\) if the bidder wins and \(0\) otherwise | Produces the simple surplus term \(v_i-b\) in the first-order condition |
| Value distributions | Independent, bidder-specific CDFs \(F_i\), with densities \(f_i\) | Makes the probability of winning depend on the rival’s distribution alone |
| Regularity | Continuous or atomless distributions, usually twice continuously differentiable with strictly positive density on a finite interval | Makes inverse strategies and derivatives well defined |
| Supports | \(v_i\in[\underline v_i,\overline v_i]\), with the simplest theory using a common or overlapping support | Determines the lower active bid and the endpoint conditions |
| Knowledge | \(F_1,F_2\), supports, independence, and auction rules are common knowledge | Defines the Bayesian game and the bidders’ correct beliefs |
| Strategies | Continuous, strictly increasing pure bidding functions wherever a type has positive winning probability | Allows each bid function to be inverted |
| Ties | A specified rule, such as uniform randomization among tied highest bidders | Is immaterial almost surely in the atomless case, but substantive with atoms or discrete values |

The risk-neutral, strictly increasing benchmark is not the only auction model that can be studied, but it is the model for which the standard inverse-bid differential system is most transparent. Maskin and Riley formulate the high-bid auction with independent types, smooth positive densities, random tie-breaking, and monotone bidding under a single-crossing condition ([Maskin and Riley’s sealed high-bid formulation](http://www.econ.ucla.edu/riley/Uni1219A.PDF)).

If the values are atomless and bidding strategies are continuous and strictly increasing, the probability of an exact tie is zero. Tie-breaking still belongs in the formal specification because it determines payoffs at off-equilibrium bids and becomes important as soon as the value distribution has atoms, the value space is discrete, or a strategy has a mass point.

Under these assumptions, the answer to the question is:

1. There is a general equilibrium characterization.
2. The characterization is a coupled inverse-bid boundary-value problem.
3. A numerical solution is normally required for arbitrary \(F_1\) and \(F_2\).
4. Closed forms exist for selected distributional families, notably two uniform distributions.
5. Existence and uniqueness are conditional on regularity and on how noncompetitive low bids, atoms, supports, and ties are treated.

Lebrun’s description remains a useful summary: explicit first-price strategies are readily available in the symmetric identically distributed case, whereas different distributions generally require numerical equilibrium computation ([Lebrun’s comparison of symmetric and asymmetric cases](https://econpapers.repec.org/paper/lvllaeccr/9923.htm)). That statement concerns arbitrary distribution pairs, not every special asymmetric family. Kaplan and Zamir later supplied a full analytic treatment for the two-uniform case ([Kaplan and Zamir, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00199-010-0563-9)).

## 2. Equilibrium characterization

### 2.1 Direct bidding strategies and inverse strategies

Let \(\beta_i(v_i)\) denote bidder \(i\)’s equilibrium bid when her value is \(v_i\). Under the monotonicity assumption, \(\beta_i\) has an inverse function

\[
\phi_i(b)=\beta_i^{-1}(b).
\]

The inverse function answers a different question: given a bid \(b\), what value type of bidder \(i\) submits that bid in equilibrium?

Working with \(\phi_i\) rather than \(\beta_i\) is the central simplification. A bidder contemplating a bid \(b\) can then calculate the probability of winning from the rival’s inverse strategy.

Suppose bidder 1 has value \(v_1\) and considers a bid \(b\) in the interval where bidder 2 is active. Bidder 1 wins whenever bidder 2’s value is below \(\phi_2(b)\). Independence therefore gives the winning probability

\[
\Pr(\text{bidder 1 wins with }b)=F_2(\phi_2(b)).
\]

Bidder 1’s expected payoff is consequently

\[
U_1(b\mid v_1)=(v_1-b)F_2(\phi_2(b)).
\]

Similarly,

\[
U_2(b\mid v_2)=(v_2-b)F_1(\phi_1(b)).
\]

These payoff expressions are the exact two-bidder counterpart of the usual symmetric auction problem. The difference is that bidder 1’s best response depends on bidder 2’s unknown inverse bid function, while bidder 2’s best response depends on bidder 1’s. The two decisions must therefore be solved jointly. This formulation appears in Maskin and Riley, Fibich and Gavious, and Hubbard and Kirkegaard ([Maskin and Riley’s best-response formulation](https://www.isid.ac.in/~dmishra/topicsdoc/maskin_riley.pdf); [Fibich and Gavious’s inverse-bid formulation](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/%7Efibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf)).

### 2.2 First-order conditions

Differentiate bidder 1’s payoff with respect to \(b\):

\[
\frac{\partial U_1(b\mid v_1)}{\partial b}=-F_2(\phi_2(b))+(v_1-b)f_2(\phi_2(b))\phi_2'(b).
\]

At an equilibrium bid, \(b=\beta_1(v_1)\), so \(v_1=\phi_1(b)\). The first-order condition becomes

\[
\frac{d}{db}\ln F_2(\phi_2(b))=\frac{1}{\phi_1(b)-b}.
\]

The analogous condition for bidder 2 is

\[
\frac{d}{db}\ln F_1(\phi_1(b))=\frac{1}{\phi_2(b)-b}.
\]

Equivalently, the inverse bidding functions satisfy the coupled system

\[
\phi_1'(b)=\frac{F_1(\phi_1(b))}{f_1(\phi_1(b))[\phi_2(b)-b]},\qquad \phi_2'(b)=\frac{F_2(\phi_2(b))}{f_2(\phi_2(b))[\phi_1(b)-b]}.
\]

The indexing is worth reading carefully. Bidder 2’s first-order condition determines \(\phi_1'\), because bidder 2’s winning probability depends on bidder 1’s inverse strategy; bidder 1’s condition determines \(\phi_2'\). This is why the system is coupled rather than two independent equations.

Fibich and Gavious derive the corresponding \(n\)-bidder system and specialize it to two bidders; Hubbard and Kirkegaard give the same active-range equations in logarithmic form ([Fibich and Gavious](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/%7Efibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf); [Hubbard and Kirkegaard](https://www.uoguelph.ca/economics/repec/workingpapers/2015/2015-02.pdf)).

The equations can also be written as a coupled integral system. For any two active bids \(b_0\) and \(b\),

\[
\ln\frac{F_1(\phi_1(b))}{F_1(\phi_1(b_0))}=\int_{b_0}^{b}\frac{ds}{\phi_2(s)-s},\qquad \ln\frac{F_2(\phi_2(b))}{F_2(\phi_2(b_0))}=\int_{b_0}^{b}\frac{ds}{\phi_1(s)-s}.
\]

This representation is useful conceptually: each bidder’s bid distribution is determined by the entire path of the rival’s inverse strategy. It is not generally an explicit integral formula because the unknown functions appear inside the integrands.

### 2.3 Why the first-order system is a boundary-value problem

The inverse system is not normally an initial-value problem with all starting values known. Instead, the lower and upper conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.

In the simplest common-support, no-reserve case, suppose both values lie on \([\underline v,\overline v]\). The standard endpoint conditions are

\[
\phi_1(\underline v)=\underline v,\qquad \phi_2(\underline v)=\underline v,
\]

at the lower active bid \(b=\underline v\), and

\[
\phi_1(\overline b)=\overline v,\qquad \phi_2(\overline b)=\overline v,
\]

at an unknown common maximum bid \(\overline b\). The unknown \(\overline b\) is a free boundary.

The common maximum bid is not an arbitrary normalization. In a nondegenerate two-bidder equilibrium, both bidders must have the same highest bid. If bidder 1’s highest bid were strictly above bidder 2’s, bidder 1’s highest type could lower her bid slightly while still beating every possible bid by bidder 2. The deviation would preserve the probability of winning and increase the surplus conditional on winning. This argument is emphasized in the exact two-bidder discussions by Hubbard and Kirkegaard and in the uniform-distribution analysis of Kaplan and Zamir ([Hubbard and Kirkegaard](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5594040ce4b0cd95241433b7/t/5d4af694a426880001550589/1565193878442/BidSeparationAugust2019.pdf); [Kaplan and Zamir](https://www.cirje.e.u-tokyo.ac.jp/research/workshops/micro/documents/March20.pdf)).

The direct bidding functions are recovered only after solving the inverse system:

\[
\beta_i(v)=\phi_i^{-1}(v).
\]

Thus the computational object is usually \(\phi_i(b)\), while the economic object of interest is \(\beta_i(v)\).

### 2.4 Interior first-order conditions are not the whole equilibrium

The ODE system characterizes the interior region in which both bidders have types who submit the relevant bids and both have positive winning probability. It does not by itself determine what happens below the lowest serious bid, above one bidder’s maximum bid in a more general multi-bidder extension, or at mass points.

A candidate inverse solution must also satisfy the global best-response problem. For each value \(v_i\), the prescribed bid must maximize

\[
(v_i-b)\Pr(\text{win}\mid b)
\]

over all feasible bids, not merely satisfy a local first-order condition. Under the standard single-crossing and monotonicity conditions, the interior first-order condition and the endpoint restrictions are often sufficient. Numerically, however, direct payoff comparisons remain important because approximation error can create a locally correct but globally unprofitable candidate.

## 3. Boundary conditions and the practical solution recipe

A usable solution method begins with the boundary conditions, not with an ODE solver. The same differential equations can produce an incorrect object if the active bid interval or endpoint treatment is wrong.

### 3.1 Step 1: Specify the two distributions

Provide:

- \(F_1,F_2\);
- densities \(f_1,f_2\);
- lower and upper support endpoints;
- any reserve or minimum bid;
- the tie-breaking rule;
- whether the supports overlap;
- and whether the intended solution is a nondegenerate pure monotone equilibrium.

For arbitrary distributions, the numerical procedure can use analytical formulas, tabulated CDFs, or numerical approximations. Gayle and Richard’s algorithm was designed to accept common analytical distributions as well as user-supplied analytical or tabulated distributions ([Gayle and Richard, 2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10614-008-9125-7)).

The density condition is computationally important. If \(f_i\) becomes zero inside the support, the ratio \(F_i/f_i\) in the inverse equations can become unstable or undefined. Gayle’s numerical treatment therefore requires densities sufficiently bounded away from zero, while the broader theory can sometimes accommodate weaker conditions through different methods ([Gayle’s numerical analysis](https://d.repec.org/n?u=RePEc:sce:scecf5:472&r=)).

### 3.2 Step 2: Identify the active bid interval

Let \(b_L\) denote the lowest bid at which a bidder has a strictly positive probability of winning and let \(\overline b\) denote the common highest bid in the nondegenerate two-bidder case.

If both supports have the same lower endpoint and there is no reserve, the standard condition is often \(b_L=\underline v\) and \(\phi_i(b_L)=\underline v\). If a reserve price \(r\) binds, types below the reserve do not submit competitive positive bids and the active boundary becomes \(\phi_i(r)=r\) in the common-support formulation. Fibich and Gavious explicitly describe the reserve-price modification as replacing the lower condition at the lower support endpoint with the condition at the reserve ([Fibich and Gavious](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/%7Efibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf)).

Unequal lower endpoints require more care. A bidder whose minimum value is higher than the other bidder’s may be able to bid below that value and still win whenever the rival’s type is low. Conversely, low types may bid their values even though they have zero winning probability. The first bid with positive winning probability is then a serious bid, and it need not equal either lower value.

For the two-uniform case, Kaplan and Zamir give an explicit lower condition. If \(\underline v_1\leq \underline v_2\) and \(m\) is a minimum bid, the active interval begins at

\[
b_L=\max\left\{\frac{\underline v_1+\underline v_2}{2},m\right\},
\]

with

\[
\phi_1(b_L)=b_L,\qquad \phi_2(b_L)=\max\{\underline v_2,m\}.
\]

These conditions are specific to the uniform model but illustrate the general principle: the lower boundary is determined by the first type that can win with positive probability, not automatically by the smallest support endpoint ([Kaplan and Zamiry, 2007](https://www.cirje.e.u-tokyo.ac.jp/research/workshops/micro/documents/March20.pdf)).

The upper conditions in the same two-uniform model are

\[
\phi_1(\overline b)=\overline v_1,\qquad \phi_2(\overline b)=\overline v_2.
\]

For exactly two bidders, these conditions use a common \(\overline b\), even when the two upper value supports differ.

### 3.3 Step 3: Solve analytically when the distributions permit it

For a general distribution pair, one should not expect an analytic solution. But several reductions are useful:

- identical distributions reduce the system to one equation;
- uniform distributions reduce the system to a tractable pair with a first integral;
- power distributions and selected other families admit special transformations;
- weak asymmetry can be treated by perturbation around a symmetric benchmark;
- a reserve price can sometimes produce a simpler lower boundary.

The symmetric reduction is instructive. With \(n\) identical bidders and common CDF \(F\),

\[
\beta_{\mathrm{sym}}(v)=v-\frac{1}{F(v)^{n-1}}\int_{\underline v}^{v}F(s)^{n-1}\,ds.
\]

For two bidders with \(F(v)=v\) on \([0,1]\),

\[
\beta_{\mathrm{sym}}(v)=\frac v2.
\]

Asymmetry prevents this one-dimensional reduction because the two bidders’ inverse strategies no longer coincide.

### 3.4 Step 4: Solve the boundary-value problem numerically

Several numerical approaches are established.

| Method | Basic procedure | Main strength | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backward shooting | Guess \(\overline b\), integrate the inverse ODEs downward, and adjust the guess until the lower boundary is met | Directly respects the free upper boundary and is conceptually simple | Can be unstable near the singular lower endpoint |
| Taylor-series shooting | Integrate backward with local recursive Taylor expansions rather than generic interpolation | High accuracy and good control near endpoint pathologies | Requires analytic or numerically generated derivatives |
| Forward or dynamical-systems methods | Start from a regularized approximation near the lower singular point and integrate toward the upper boundary | Can avoid the inherent instability of backward shooting | Requires careful treatment of admissible directions at the singular point |
| Collocation or projection | Approximate \(\phi_i\) with Chebyshev, polynomial, spline, or finite-element bases and minimize ODE and boundary residuals | Handles free boundaries and shape constraints flexibly | Approximation error depends on basis choice and grid |
| Discretized equilibrium algorithms | Discretize values and bids and solve for approximate best responses or strategy distributions | Useful when smooth pure strategies fail or the model is more general | Produces an approximate discretized equilibrium and requires convergence checks |

Backward shooting is the traditional method. Bajari describes guessing the unknown endpoint, integrating the inverse-bid equations, and adjusting the guess until the known boundary is met; his implementation uses standard Runge–Kutta methods ([Bajari’s shooting construction](https://kylewoodward.com/blog-data/pdfs/references/bajari-economic-theory-2001A.pdf)). Fibich and Gavious use the same basic free-boundary idea, with backward integration and adjustment of \(\overline b\) until the lower residual is below a prescribed tolerance such as \(10^{-5}\) in their simulations ([Fibich and Gavious](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/%7Efibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf)).

Marshall, Meurer, Richard, and Stromquist instead use backward piecewise low-order Taylor expansions. In their implementation, \(10{,}000\) subintervals, Taylor order \(5\), and convergence parameters of roughly \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-8}\) were adequate for their numerical examples, but those values are reported implementation choices rather than universal accuracy requirements ([Marshall et al.](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf)).

Gayle and Richard develop a closely related automated local Taylor-series algorithm for arbitrary supplied distributions. Their method computes inverse equilibrium functions and auxiliary statistics, including revenue and winning probabilities, rather than requiring a separate multidimensional integration over direct bids ([Gayle and Richard, 2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10614-008-9125-7)).

Backward shooting is not numerically innocuous. Marshall et al. report that forward integration is attracted to linear “nuisance” solutions that fail the terminal conditions, while backward solutions become unstable near the origin. Fibich and Gavish use a dynamical-systems analysis to explain this instability and propose stable forward-shooting and no-shooting alternatives; in the two-type case, their formulation is particularly simple ([Marshall et al.](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf); [Fibich and Gavish, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.1110.0535)).

Collocation is a useful alternative when shooting is poorly conditioned. One approximates

\[
\phi_i(b)\approx\sum_{k=0}^{K}\alpha_{ik}T_k(x(b)),
\]

where \(T_k\) are Chebyshev polynomials and \(x(b)\) maps the active bid interval into \([-1,1]\). The coefficients and the free boundary are chosen so that the ODE residuals vanish at collocation nodes and the endpoint conditions are satisfied. The numerical review by Hubbard and Paarsch describes projection, spectral, and finite-element methods of this type and stresses that the free-boundary conditions must be imposed directly or included in the objective ([Hubbard and Paarsch review](https://www.carloalberto.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/no.291.pdf)).

### 3.5 Step 5: Recover the direct bidding functions

Once the inverse curves are computed, invert each monotone curve numerically:

\[
\beta_i(v)=\phi_i^{-1}(v).
\]

Interpolation should preserve monotonicity. A nonmonotone interpolant can create artificial profitable deviations even if the underlying inverse solution is valid.

For uniform distributions, analytic inversion may be available. For arbitrary distributions, monotone interpolation on a sufficiently fine grid is usually adequate, provided that the numerical solution is refined and independently checked.

### 3.6 Step 6: Validate equilibrium rather than only solving equations

A credible numerical solution should pass several distinct tests.

First, evaluate the two ODE residuals across the entire active bid grid. The residuals should be small relative to the scale of the equations, not merely at the endpoints.

Second, evaluate the boundary residuals. In the common-support case, these include

\[
\phi_i(b_L)-\underline v
\]

and

\[
\phi_i(\overline b)-\overline v.
\]

With unequal supports, use the appropriate lower serious-bid targets and \(\phi_i(\overline b)=\overline v_i\).

Third, check monotonicity, positivity of the relevant denominators, and the ordering \(b<\phi_i(b)\) on the interior region where a type bidding \(b\) earns positive surplus. Violations usually indicate an incorrect boundary condition or a failed numerical step.

Fourth, perform direct best-response checks. For a grid of values \(v_i\), calculate

\[
U_i(b\mid v_i)=(v_i-b)\Pr(\text{win}\mid b)
\]

over bids below, inside, and above the computed active interval. The prescribed bid \(\beta_i(v_i)\) should attain the maximum up to the numerical tolerance. This check is stronger than checking the first-order condition because it detects profitable deviations to regions where the interior ODE was not applied.

Fifth, refine the grid, Taylor order, or polynomial degree. A valid approximation should stabilize as numerical resolution increases. One should also compare at least two methods when the endpoint is highly singular—for example, backward Taylor shooting and collocation.

Finally, use known special cases as unit tests. A solver should converge to \(\beta(v)=v/2\) when \(F_1=F_2=U[0,1]\), and should reproduce the analytic two-uniform solution when the distributions are uniform on different intervals.

## 4. Existence, uniqueness, and their limits

### 4.1 What the foundational theorems establish

The foundational literature does not say that every conceivable asymmetric auction has a unique smooth pure equilibrium. It establishes existence and uniqueness under specified restrictions.

Lebrun’s existence result covers independent private values and gives a particularly transparent sufficient condition: the value supports have the same minimum and that minimum is not a mass point of any distribution ([Lebrun’s existence result](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Existence-of-an-equilibrium-in-first-price-auctions-Lebrun/20023ac9d5607a82987264024d7a23d21c4fc5b0)). This is an existence condition, not a general closed-form solution and not a universal uniqueness theorem.

Maskin and Riley’s work establishes monotone equilibrium properties for sealed high-bid auctions under smooth distributions, no overbidding, and single crossing. In their two-buyer uniqueness result, Assumption 1—which rules out bids above reservation values—is sufficient for uniqueness within the relevant equilibrium class ([Maskin and Riley’s uniqueness proposition](http://www.econ.ucla.edu/riley/Uni1219A.PDF)).

Lebrun’s later uniqueness analysis treats broader asymmetric settings, but adds distributional regularity near the lower endpoint. A common formulation is that the reverse hazard rate \(f_i(v)/F_i(v)\) is strictly decreasing near the lower support endpoint, equivalently a suitable strict log-concavity condition. Hubbard and Kirkegaard summarize this condition as strict log-concavity near \(\underline v_i\) and assume an essentially unique equilibrium in undominated strategies ([Hubbard and Kirkegaard](https://www.uoguelph.ca/economics/repec/workingpapers/2015/2015-02.pdf)).

These results should be read as conditional statements:

| Result | Typical conditions | What it supports | What it does not imply |
|---|---|---|---|
| Existence | Independent values, common lower endpoint, no mass at that endpoint, or related regularity | A Nash equilibrium exists | A smooth pure monotone equilibrium exists under every support configuration |
| Two-bidder uniqueness | No overbidding, single crossing, monotonicity, and appropriate endpoint treatment | Uniqueness of the relevant active or undominated equilibrium | Uniqueness of arbitrary zero-winning behavior below the active interval |
| Lebrun-style uniqueness | Strict log-concavity or decreasing reverse hazard near lower endpoints | Essentially unique equilibrium under broader asymmetric supports | Unconditional uniqueness with atoms, discontinuities, or unbounded supports |
| Numerical uniqueness | A solver converges to one residual-minimizing solution | Evidence about a computed candidate | A mathematical uniqueness proof |

The apparent differences among sources usually concern the equilibrium class and the treatment of noncompetitive bids. A theorem about uniqueness in undominated strategies need not rule out strategically irrelevant variations among types that have zero probability of winning.

### 4.2 Lower endpoints and singular behavior

The lower endpoint is the most delicate part of the smooth ODE formulation.

When both supports begin at zero and \(F_i(0)=0\), the inverse equations contain expressions whose limiting form is effectively \(0/0\). Fibich and Gavish describe the common-support boundary-value problem as nonstandard because the right-hand side is singular at \(b=0\), so the ordinary local existence theorem for an initial-value problem cannot simply be applied there ([Fibich and Gavish](http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/Asymmetric-first-price-auctions-boundary-layer.pdf)).

This explains several numerical phenomena:

- forward integration can converge to an inadmissible linear solution;
- backward integration can become unstable near the origin;
- a small error in the guessed maximum bid can explode as the solver approaches the lower boundary;
- starting the calculation exactly at the singular endpoint can be less reliable than starting at a small positive distance using a series expansion.

A robust implementation therefore uses one of three devices:

1. derive a local asymptotic or Taylor expansion near the lower endpoint;
2. introduce a small positive starting point and control the resulting endpoint error;
3. reformulate the system in variables such as \(F_i(\phi_i(b))\), logarithms, or dynamical-system coordinates.

The lower endpoint can also cease to be singular if a reserve price or an atom makes the relevant CDF positive at the first active bid. That does not make the economics trivial; it changes the boundary condition.

### 4.3 Unequal lower supports

Unequal lower supports do not automatically invalidate the method, but they invalidate the careless use of the common-lower-endpoint condition.

Suppose \(\underline v_1<\underline v_2\). Low types of bidder 1 may submit bids that never win because bidder 2’s minimum value is high enough to sustain a higher competitive bid. The first bidder type with positive winning probability may therefore lie above \(\underline v_1\). Bidder 2’s lowest winning type may in turn bid below \(\underline v_2\), because she can win when bidder 1 draws a low value.

The solution must then include a nonwinning lower region and an active region joined at a serious bid \(b_L\). For the uniform case, this gives the explicit lower boundary described above. For arbitrary distributions, \(b_L\) is determined by the relevant best-response and indifference conditions; it should not be guessed from the supports alone.

A particularly important limiting case is disjoint support. Quint’s asymmetric example takes the weak bidder’s value as \(U[0,1]\) and the strong bidder’s value as \(U[2,3]\). The reported equilibrium has the weak bidder bid her type while the strong bidder bids \(1\) regardless of her value, wins for sure, and pays \(1\). The lecture explicitly notes that this equilibrium is not characterized by the ordinary interior first-order-condition system because the support separation creates a boundary case ([Quint’s asymmetric-auction lecture](https://users.ssc.wisc.edu/~dquint/econ805%202007/econ%20805%20lecture%209.pdf)).

This example is not a generic formula for all disjoint-support auctions. It demonstrates why the ODE must be applied only where both bidders are genuinely active.

### 4.4 Unequal upper supports

For exactly two bidders in a nondegenerate monotone equilibrium, unequal upper value supports do not by themselves imply different maximum bids. The two highest types still share a common highest bid. If one highest bid were higher, its bidder could lower it while preserving certain victory.

The situation changes when there are more than two bidders divided into asymmetric groups. For example, if there are multiple strong bidders, a strong bidder’s maximum bid can exceed the weak group’s maximum bid without losing the auction to a rival strong bidder. The inverse-bid equations then change above the weak group’s highest bid because only the strong group remains active.

This distinction matters because results about “bid separation” or “bid bifurcation” in the multi-bidder literature should not be imported into the exact two-bidder model. Hubbard and Kirkegaard report that with three strong and two weak uniform bidders, bid supports separate when the strong upper support exceeds the weak upper support by more than \(8.11\%\). That threshold is a five-bidder result, not a two-bidder result ([Hubbard and Kirkegaard](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5594040ce4b0cd95241433b7/t/5d4af694a426880001550589/1565193878442/BidSeparationAugust2019.pdf)).

In the multi-bidder extension, the common active-range equation is replaced above the weak group’s maximum bid by an equation involving only the remaining strong rivals. A solver that imposes one common maximum bid globally can then produce a wrong solution or fail to converge. For the requested two-bidder model, however, the standard common-maximum condition remains the appropriate nondegenerate boundary.

### 4.5 Multiplicity below the lowest winning bid

Even when the active equilibrium is unique, bids that never win may be underdetermined. Maskin and Riley give an unequal-support example with one bidder uniform on \([0,1]\) and the other on \([3,4]\). One equilibrium has the strong bidder bid \(1\) and the weak bidder bid her value; the weak bidder’s strategy can be altered below the lowest winning bid without changing any winning probability or payoff. The resulting multiplicity concerns zero-winning-probability behavior, not the active competitive equilibrium ([Maskin and Riley’s unequal-support example](https://www.ias.edu/sites/default/files/sss/papers/econpaper31.pdf)).

This is why applied work often imposes an undominated-strategy or trembling-hand refinement: a type that cannot win may be assigned a natural bid, such as her value, without claiming that every off-path bid is uniquely determined by equilibrium.

## 5. The two-uniform example and the symmetric benchmark

### 5.1 The symmetric benchmark

With two iid bidders whose values are \(U[0,1]\), the unique increasing equilibrium is

\[
\beta_1(v)=\beta_2(v)=\frac v2.
\]

A bidder shades her value because a higher bid raises the probability of winning but lowers the surplus conditional on winning. With two symmetric bidders, the trade-off produces a constant one-half shading factor.

The symmetric formula is more generally

\[
\beta_{\mathrm{sym}}(v)=v-\frac{1}{F(v)}\int_{\underline v}^{v}F(s)\,ds
\]

for two bidders. The asymmetric problem cannot usually be reduced to this formula because each bidder faces a different bid distribution.

### 5.2 Arbitrary uniform intervals

Let bidder 1’s value be uniform on \([\underline v_1,\overline v_1]\), bidder 2’s value be uniform on \([\underline v_2,\overline v_2]\), and assume \(\underline v_1\leq\underline v_2\). On the active interval, the inverse equations simplify because

\[
\frac{F_i(v)}{f_i(v)}=v-\underline v_i.
\]

The system becomes

\[
\phi_1'(b)[\phi_2(b)-b]=\phi_1(b)-\underline v_1,\qquad \phi_2'(b)[\phi_1(b)-b]=\phi_2(b)-\underline v_2.
\]

With a minimum bid \(m\), the lower active boundary is

\[
b_L=\max\left\{\frac{\underline v_1+\underline v_2}{2},m\right\},
\]

with

\[
\phi_1(b_L)=b_L,\qquad \phi_2(b_L)=\max\{\underline v_2,m\}.
\]

The system has the first integral

\[
\phi_1(b)\phi_2(b)=b[\phi_1(b)+\phi_2(b)]-(\underline v_1+\underline v_2)b+c,
\]

where

\[
c=\frac{(\underline v_1+\underline v_2)^2}{4}\quad\text{if }m\leq\frac{\underline v_1+\underline v_2}{2},
\]

and

\[
c=(\underline v_1+\underline v_2)m-m^2\quad\text{if }m>\frac{\underline v_1+\underline v_2}{2}.
\]

The common maximum bid is therefore

\[
\overline b=\frac{\overline v_1\overline v_2-c}{(\overline v_1-\underline v_1)+(\overline v_2-\underline v_2)}.
\]

Kaplan and Zamir use this reduction to obtain analytic inverse and direct bidding functions for every nontrivial two-uniform parameterization, with and without a binding minimum bid. Their paper also proves continuity of the equilibrium in the support endpoints and the minimum bid ([Kaplan and Zamir, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00199-010-0563-9); [Kaplan and Zamiry’s analytic manuscript](https://www.cirje.e.u-tokyo.ac.jp/research/workshops/micro/documents/March20.pdf)).

For the especially transparent case \(\underline v_1=\underline v_2=0\), no reserve, and \(\overline v_2\geq\overline v_1\), the common maximum bid is

\[
\overline b=\frac{\overline v_1\overline v_2}{\overline v_1+\overline v_2}.
\]

The inverse strategies are

\[
\phi_1(b)=\frac{2b\overline v_1^2\overline v_2^2}{\overline v_1^2\overline v_2^2+b^2(\overline v_2^2-\overline v_1^2)},\qquad \phi_2(b)=\frac{2b\overline v_1^2\overline v_2^2}{\overline v_1^2\overline v_2^2-b^2(\overline v_2^2-\overline v_1^2)}.
\]

When \(\overline v_1=\overline v_2\), both expressions reduce to \(\phi_i(b)=2b\), hence \(\beta_i(v)=v/2\). When bidder 2 has the larger upper support, \(\phi_2(b)>\phi_1(b)\) at a common bid. Equivalently, at a common value in the overlapping range, bidder 2’s direct bid is lower: the stronger bidder shades more.

The uniform case also contains a simple class with linear asymmetric bids. For suitable values and a minimum bid \(m\), Kaplan and Zamiry obtain

\[
\phi_1(b)=2b-m,\qquad \phi_2(b)=2b-\frac m2,
\]

or, on the active range,

\[
\beta_1(v)=\frac{v+m}{2},\qquad \beta_2(v)=\frac v2+\frac m4.
\]

This is an exact special case, not evidence that asymmetric bids are generally linear. The same paper shows that linearity is restricted to particular relationships among the lower endpoints, minimum bid, and upper-support lengths.

### 5.3 Binding minimum bids and degenerate regions

A minimum bid can change the equilibrium qualitatively rather than merely shift every bid upward. In the uniform model, the lower endpoint changes when \(m=(\underline v_1+\underline v_2)/2\), and additional changes occur when the minimum bid reaches one bidder’s lower value. Kaplan and Zamiry also show that the minimum bid can produce bid-function crossings even when one distribution stochastically dominates the other over the relevant conditional range.

Some parameter regions do not support the nontrivial interior equilibrium described by the inverse ODE. In their uniform analysis:

- if \(m\geq\min\{\overline v_1,\overline v_2\}\), there is a trivial equilibrium in which at most one bidder bids at the minimum;
- if the higher lower endpoint is sufficiently large relative to the other bidder’s upper endpoint, one bidder can be so dominant that she always bids the other bidder’s upper value and wins.

In the notation of the source, if \(\underline v_2\geq2\overline v_1-\underline v_1\), bidder 2 always bids \(\overline v_1\). This is the “Getty effect,” named for an extreme case in which one bidder is effectively certain to win ([Kaplan and Zamiry](https://www.cirje.e.u-tokyo.ac.jp/research/workshops/micro/documents/March20.pdf)).

These cases are not failures of equilibrium theory. They are cases in which the assumed interior competitive structure is absent, so the correct solution is a boundary or dominant-bid equilibrium rather than a globally active two-equation ODE solution.

### 5.4 How asymmetry changes bids

The direction of bid shading depends on how the distributions differ.

Maskin and Riley analyze a stretched-uniform comparison in which the weak bidder is uniform on \([0,1/(1+z)]\) and the strong bidder is uniform on \([0,1/(1-z)]\), with \(z>0\). At \(z=0\), both distributions are \(U[0,1]\) and the inverse bid is \(2b\). When \(z>0\), the strong bidder reduces her bid relative to the symmetric benchmark at a common value, while the weak bidder bids more aggressively ([Maskin and Riley’s stretched-uniform comparison](https://www.isid.ac.in/~dmishra/topicsdoc/maskin_riley.pdf)).

The intuition is strategic. A strong bidder expects higher values and is less concerned about losing to the weak bidder at moderate bids. She can therefore extract more surplus by shading. The weak bidder faces a stronger rival and must compensate with more aggressive bidding. This does not mean that the weak bidder bids more at every possible value in every asymmetric model; it is a result under appropriate stochastic-ordering conditions.

Fibich and Gavious state the two-bidder comparison using conditional stochastic dominance. If \(F_1/F_2\) is increasing, bidder 1 is stronger in the relevant sense and the equilibrium satisfies \(\beta_1(v)<\beta_2(v)\) on the common interior value range. Their result also emphasizes that the directional comparison requires a distributional ordering; it cannot be generalized to every pair \(F_1\neq F_2\) ([Fibich and Gavious](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/%7Efibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf)).

### 5.5 A weak-asymmetry perturbation example

A useful analytic approximation starts from the symmetric uniform benchmark on \([0,1]\) and perturbs the two CDFs:

\[
F_1(v)=v-\varepsilon v(1-v),\qquad F_2(v)=v+\varepsilon v(1-v).
\]

For \(\varepsilon>0\), bidder 1 has the lower CDF on the interior and is therefore stronger in the relevant stochastic-ordering sense. Fibich and Gavious obtain the first-order approximations

\[
\beta_1(v)\approx\frac v2-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(v^2-v^3),\qquad \beta_2(v)\approx\frac v2+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(v^2-v^3).
\]

The stronger bidder shades below \(v/2\), while the weaker bidder bids above \(v/2\). These are perturbation formulas, not exact equilibrium bids for arbitrary \(\varepsilon\). The paper reports that the approximation and exact numerical solution are indistinguishable at \(\varepsilon=0.1\) and \(0.25\), remain remarkably close at \(\varepsilon=0.5\) despite that value being outside the formal weak-asymmetry range, and generate revenue approximations with errors below \(1\%\) in the reported examples ([Fibich and Gavious’s perturbation computations](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/%7Efibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf)).

The example illustrates both the usefulness and the limit of analytical approximations. They can explain the local mechanism by which asymmetry changes bids, but they do not replace solving the exact boundary-value problem when asymmetry is large or the distributions have substantially different supports.

### 5.6 Revenue and allocation implications

In the symmetric IPV model, the first-price allocation is efficient because the highest value produces the highest bid. With asymmetric distributions, bid rankings need not coincide with value rankings. A weaker bidder can bid more aggressively than a stronger bidder at the same value, and the resulting allocation can be inefficient.

Revenue comparisons are also conditional. Maskin and Riley obtain first-price revenue dominance over the open auction under particular stochastic-ordering assumptions, while other distributional configurations can reverse the ranking. Gayle’s numerical study finds first-price revenue above second-price revenue in several first-order-stochastically ordered environments, but also reports cases in which CDFs cross and second-price revenue is higher. The source explicitly cautions that a bid-function crossing does not imply a universal revenue ranking ([Gayle’s numerical study](https://d.repec.org/n?u=RePEc:sce:scecf5:472&r=)).

For weak asymmetry, Fibich and Gavious show that first- and second-price revenues differ only at second order in the asymmetry parameter in their perturbation framework. That is an approximation result around symmetry, not a universal revenue-equivalence theorem for arbitrary asymmetric distributions ([Fibich and Gavious](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/%7Efibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf)).

## 6. What changes under irregular distributions or relaxed assumptions?

### 6.1 Atoms and mass points

Atoms change the problem in two ways. First, a bid can tie with positive probability. Second, the winning probability becomes discontinuous at mass points, so an ordinary derivative-based first-order condition may not describe a best response.

Maskin and Riley explicitly allow a mass point at the lower endpoint, potentially caused by a reserve price. At the lower bid, winning probabilities then include the probability mass at the endpoint, and the boundary equations must incorporate those probabilities rather than treating them as zero ([Maskin and Riley’s lower-end mass point treatment](https://www.isid.ac.in/~dmishra/topicsdoc/maskin_riley.pdf)).

Kaplan and Zamiry show that their uniform-with-minimum-bid solution can also be interpreted as covering certain lower-end atoms. If a uniform distribution begins at a lower value below the minimum bid, the values below the minimum are effectively pooled at the minimum competitive bid. The bidder behavior in the atomistic interpretation requires care because the convention that a zero-winning-probability type bids her value may need to be relaxed ([Kaplan and Zamiry](https://www.cirje.e.u-tokyo.ac.jp/research/workshops/micro/documents/March20.pdf)).

With atoms, the tie-breaking rule is not cosmetic. It affects each bidder’s payoff at a mass bid and can determine whether a pure equilibrium exists. A theorem or numerical method that assumes atomless values and zero-probability ties cannot simply be reused.

### 6.2 Discrete values

For finite discrete value distributions, bidding functions need not be smooth or strictly increasing in the continuous sense. A value may optimally randomize over bids, bid supports need not be connected, and a tie-breaking rule can be essential.

Wang, Shen, and Zuo formulate a discrete first-price auction with publicly known bidder-specific value distributions, quasi-linear utilities, simultaneous nonnegative bids, and no overbidding. They provide an algorithm and prove existence and uniqueness under their discrete-model assumptions, while emphasizing that continuous-value uniqueness results do not automatically transfer to the discrete case ([Wang, Shen, and Zuo](https://www.weiran-shen.info/page_files/bayesian_nash_equilibrium_in_first-price_auction_with_discrete_value_distributions.pdf)).

Their discrete formulation uses a Vickrey auction among the highest bidders to break ties. They state that this tie-breaking assumption is unnecessary in the continuous setting but needed in the discrete setting to address best-response problems. Without the specified rule, their algorithm produces an approximate rather than exact Bayesian Nash equilibrium.

McFadden’s two-bidder example makes the need for mixed strategies concrete. One bidder has value \(400\); the other has value \(300\) or \(800\) with equal probability, with a reserve of \(300\). A proposed pure strategy for the high-value state is profitable to deviate from, and the equilibrium involves bid distributions over an interval rather than two smooth pure bidding functions ([McFadden’s discrete asymmetric example](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~mcfadden/eC103_f03/auctionlect.pdf)).

The correct response to discrete values is therefore not to force the continuous ODE system onto a finite grid. One should formulate the finite Bayesian game directly, specify tie-breaking, solve the finite best-response conditions, and verify the resulting mixed or pure equilibrium.

### 6.3 Risk aversion

Risk neutrality is sufficient for the simple surplus term \(v_i-b\), but not necessary for every monotone-equilibrium method.

If bidder \(i\)’s utility from winning with surplus \(x\) is \(U_i(x)\), her payoff from pretending to have type \(y\) and bidding \(\beta_i(y)\) is

\[
U_i(v_i-\beta_i(y))F_j(\phi_j(\beta_i(y))).
\]

The first-order condition changes from the risk-neutral expression to a condition involving the marginal utility ratio:

\[
\frac{d}{db}\ln F_j(\phi_j(b))=\frac{U_i'(\phi_i(b)-b)}{U_i(\phi_i(b)-b)}.
\]

The equations remain coupled, but the right-hand side is no longer simply \(1/(\phi_i(b)-b)\). Risk aversion can also alter endpoint conditions, especially with reserves or entry. The 2025 work of Chen, Gentry, Li, and Lu studies risk aversion and selective entry and shows that parameter-dependent bid supports make both identification and computation nonregular ([Chen et al., 2025](https://www.restud.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/MS20719manuscript.pdf)).

For the question posed here, risk neutrality is the appropriate baseline because it isolates ex-ante distributional asymmetry. If risk preferences are also asymmetric, one must distinguish distributional effects from preference effects.

### 6.4 Correlation and interdependent values

Independence is what permits the simple winning probability \(F_j(\phi_j(b))\). If values are correlated, bidder \(i\)’s winning probability conditional on \(v_i\) is instead a conditional probability such as

\[
\Pr(v_j\leq\phi_j(b)\mid v_i).
\]

The derivative of that expression may involve the joint density and the bidder’s own type. The two equations no longer have the simple factorized form above.

Interdependent values require still more changes because a bidder’s payoff from winning can depend on information about the rival’s value or signal. The standard IPV inverse-bid method is therefore not a universal auction algorithm; it is a method tied to the independent private-value structure.

### 6.5 Unbounded supports and weak regularity

Finite support is convenient because it supplies a common upper boundary. If supports are unbounded, there may be no finite \(\overline b\) from which to shoot. Maskin and Riley conjecture that unbounded support can generate a continuum of asymmetric equilibria, illustrating why finite-support assumptions are more than a technical convenience ([Maskin and Riley](https://www.ias.edu/sites/default/files/sss/papers/econpaper31.pdf)).

If densities vanish, are discontinuous, or have complicated endpoint behavior, the ratio \(F_i/f_i\) can become ill-conditioned. The equilibrium may still exist, but the standard smooth ODE implementation may need a variable transformation, a piecewise treatment, or a fully discretized method.

### 6.6 Exact two bidders versus more than two

The requested model has exactly two bidders. That restriction is analytically important.

With exactly two bidders, a nondegenerate monotone equilibrium has a common maximum bid even when the upper value supports differ. With more than two bidders, a group of strong bidders can continue competing against one another after weaker bidders have reached their maximum bid. The bid support can then split into an overlapping region and a high-bid region in which only one group is active.

Hubbard and Kirkegaard call this phenomenon bid separation or bid bifurcation. Their solution modifies the standard method by first diagnosing whether the supports separate and then solving different ODE systems over the relevant bid regions. In their notation, the common active-region system is replaced in the high region by an equation involving only the strong group’s remaining rivals ([Hubbard and Kirkegaard, 2019](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5594040ce4b0cd95241433b7/t/5d4af694a426880001550589/1565193878442/BidSeparationAugust2019.pdf)).

This is a limitation of extensions beyond two bidders, not a reason to abandon the standard common-maximum boundary in the exact two-bidder problem. It does, however, warn against treating “two asymmetric bidders” and “two asymmetric groups with many bidders” as the same computational problem.

### 6.7 General-purpose computational methods

The inverse-ODE method exploits smooth monotone pure strategies. When those assumptions are doubtful, a more general discretized equilibrium method can be useful.

Bichler, Fichtl, and Oberlechner describe auctions as Bayesian games with continuous type and action spaces and note that exact equilibrium computation is computationally hard in general. Their method discretizes types and actions and learns distributional strategies through online optimization. If the algorithm converges to a pure strategy, it obtains a high-precision approximate equilibrium of the discretized game, and the authors provide evidence that the discretized equilibrium approximates an equilibrium of the continuous game ([Bichler, Fichtl, and Oberlechner](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/opre.2022.0287)).

This method is broader than the smooth two-bidder IPV problem and should not be confused with an analytic solution of the inverse ODE. It is most useful when the model includes interdependent values, unusual utilities, discontinuities, or strategy shapes that are not known in advance.

Recent existence work also emphasizes that the atomless, independent, risk-neutral model is not the frontier of first-price auction theory. Olszewski, Reny, and Siegel provide sufficient conditions accommodating non-quasi-linear utility, atoms, and positive or negative correlation, and show that changing tie-breaking at a critical lower-support statistic can restore existence in cases where standard tie-breaking does not ([Olszewski, Reny, and Siegel, 2026](https://doi.org/10.3982/ecta22570)). These results broaden the existence theory; they do not eliminate the need to choose a computational method appropriate to the primitives.

## 7. A practical decision guide

The appropriate method depends on what is being held fixed.

| Environment | Equilibrium object | Recommended method | Main qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| Two smooth asymmetric IPV bidders, overlapping supports | Two monotone inverse bid functions and a common maximum bid | Coupled inverse ODE with shooting, stable forward integration, or collocation | Endpoint conditions must be correct |
| Two uniform distributions on arbitrary intervals | Analytic inverse and direct bid functions | Kaplan–Zamir formulas | Exclude trivial or dominant-bid regions when using the interior formula |
| Weak asymmetry around a symmetric model | Approximate direct bids and comparative statics | Perturbation expansion | Accuracy is formal only for weak asymmetry |
| Unequal lower supports or a reserve | Active-region inverse functions with a serious-bid boundary | Piecewise boundary-value method | Low types may submit zero-winning bids |
| Atoms or discrete values | Pure or mixed finite/discontinuous strategies | Discrete Bayesian-game algorithm or mixed-strategy analysis | Tie-breaking becomes substantive |
| Correlated or interdependent values | Conditional winning probabilities based on joint distributions | Modified integral or fixed-point system | The simple factorization into \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) fails |
| More than two asymmetric bidders | Potentially separated bid-support regions | Region-by-region ODE or collocation method | A common maximum bid may be wrong |

For the exact model in the question, the standard workflow is therefore:

1. Specify \(F_1,F_2\), their supports, and any reserve or minimum bid.

2. Determine whether both bidders are active on a common competitive bid interval and derive the correct lower serious-bid condition.

3. Impose the common upper bid condition \(\phi_i(\overline b)=\overline v_i\).

4. Solve the coupled inverse-bid ODE system analytically if the distributions permit it; otherwise solve the free-boundary problem numerically.

5. Invert the monotone inverse curves to obtain \(\beta_1,\beta_2\).

6. Check residuals, endpoint conditions, monotonicity, convergence, and all-type best responses.

The most common conceptual error is to solve the interior equations with an endpoint condition borrowed from the symmetric model. The most common numerical error is to treat a residual-minimizing approximation as an equilibrium without checking deviations outside the active grid.

## 8. Historical development and scholarly landmarks

The literature developed through a sequence of transitions.

The symmetric benchmark was solved first because identical distributions collapse the equilibrium problem to one scalar differential equation and yield a direct integral formula. Vickrey’s 1961 work introduced important asymmetric uniform cases, but the general two-uniform problem remained open for decades. Kaplan and Zamir describe this history and present the general analytic solution for two uniform distributions ([Kaplan and Zamir](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00199-010-0563-9)).

The next transition was theoretical. Lebrun and Maskin and Riley established existence, monotonicity, and uniqueness results for asymmetric first-price auctions under suitable regularity conditions. This made numerical computation meaningful: researchers could calculate the equilibrium selected by the theory rather than merely search for arbitrary fixed points. Marshall et al. summarize the early existence and uniqueness contributions and explain why the resulting differential equations were generally analytically intractable ([Marshall et al.](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf)).

The third transition was computational. Marshall et al. developed backward recursive Taylor-series methods for the two-point boundary-value problem. Fibich and Gavious later used perturbation analysis to obtain transparent approximate bid functions and improved numerical revenue calculations. Gayle and Richard supplied an automated implementation that accommodates arbitrary analytical or tabulated distributions.

The fourth transition concerned numerical stability. The singular lower endpoint and the instability of naive shooting motivated dynamical-systems methods, stable forward shooting, and collocation. The more recent numerical literature also emphasizes that the endpoint and support structure should be treated as part of the equilibrium problem rather than as incidental numerical details.

The fifth transition concerns the scope of the model. Work on unequal supports and more than two bidders shows that a common maximum bid is not always valid outside the exact two-bidder setting. Work on discrete values, atoms, risk aversion, correlation, and general computational equilibrium methods extends the theory in other directions.

The principal scholarly landmarks are:

| Source | Main contribution | Status for the requested model |
|---|---|---|
| Vickrey (1961) | Early asymmetric first-price uniform cases and the motivating analytic problem | Historical precursor |
| Lebrun (1996) | Existence for independent private-value first-price auctions under lower-endpoint conditions | Existence foundation |
| Maskin and Riley (1996, 2000) | Monotone equilibrium characterization, two-bidder uniqueness results, strong-versus-weak bid shading, and revenue comparisons | Foundational theory |
| Marshall, Meurer, Richard, and Stromquist (1994) | Numerical solution of asymmetric first-price boundary-value systems using backward Taylor expansions | Foundational computation |
| Lebrun (1999, 2006) | Asymmetric \(N\)-bidder characterization and conditional uniqueness under lower-endpoint regularity | Broader existence and uniqueness theory |
| Fibich and Gavious (2003) | Perturbation approximations, inverse-bid equations, and numerical revenue methods | Analytical approximation and computation |
| Gayle and Richard (2008) | Automated numerical computation for arbitrary supplied distributions | Practical implementation |
| Kaplan and Zamir (2012) | Analytic solution for two bidders with arbitrary uniform intervals and minimum bids | Main closed-form special case |
| Fibich and Gavish (2012, 2015) | Dynamical-systems analysis, stable forward methods, and free-boundary treatment of singular ODEs | Numerical stability |
| Hubbard and Kirkegaard (2015, 2019) | Unequal-support complications and bid separation beyond the exact two-bidder case | Extension and warning |
| Bichler, Fichtl, and Oberlechner (2023; published in the 2025 issue) | Discretized general-purpose computation of approximate Bayesian equilibria | Broader computational alternative |
| Olszewski, Reny, and Siegel (2026) | Existence with atoms, correlation, and non-quasi-linear utilities | Broader existence boundary |

## Conclusion

For two bidders with independent private values drawn from different distributions, the general solution method is well established:

- write each bidder’s expected payoff using the rival’s inverse bidding function;
- derive the two coupled inverse-bid first-order conditions;
- impose the correct lower serious-bid and common upper-bid conditions;
- solve the resulting boundary-value problem analytically in special cases or numerically otherwise;
- invert the inverse strategies and verify global best responses.

The method is general as an equilibrium characterization, not as a universal closed-form formula. Smooth atomless distributions, common knowledge, risk neutrality, and monotone pure strategies yield the standard coupled ODE approach. Unequal lower supports require special lower-boundary treatment; atoms and discrete values require explicit tie-breaking and often mixed strategies; correlation or non-quasi-linear utility changes the equations; and more than two bidders can invalidate the common-maximum boundary through bid separation. Within the exact two-bidder asymmetric IPV model, however, solving a coupled inverse-bid boundary-value problem is the standard general answer.
